children: Mixo Das, Asia Equity and Quant Strategist at JPMorgan, expects equity markets across Asia, including India, to remain volatile over the next four to six weeks as investors navigate geopolitical tensions, oil price uncertainty and global interest rate moves.
Despite the near-term outlook, the brokerage continues to favour artificial intelligence (AI)-linked stocks and financials, while maintaining a neutral allocation on India.

Speaking from the sidelines of the JPMorgan India Conference, Das said seasonal factors, uncertainty around oil prices and the upcoming US midterm elections could keep markets under pressure in the near term. However, he said the broader backdrop for Asian equities remains supportive because of earnings growth, reasonable valuations and light investor positioning.
He added that the firm's longer-term view on equities remains constructive.

"If you step back a little bit and you look at the broader picture, you still have earnings in Asia going up very strongly... So all in all, the equity setup both in Asia and in regional markets is pretty positive," he said.

Das said the performance of AI-linked stocks will depend on whether companies can successfully monetise artificial intelligence investments. He said software developers, application providers and AI model companies will need to demonstrate revenue generation before the benefits flow through the broader technology ecosystem.

"So, the longer this AI boost can continue, the longer these AI stocks will continue to perform," he said, adding, "At this point, with the data that we have today and with our expectations in the next few years, we are very comfortable that the AI stocks will probably continue to do well."
This is an edited transcript of the interview.

Q: Just the way the markets are set up right now, all of last week, we did see a lot of uncertainty around, you know, the geopolitical developments. Despite that, oil was contained. We did see the US Fed and the BoJ hike rates. Again, that was as expected, rather than feared, and there is one more hike coming towards the end of this year as well, which is what the expectation is. Amidst all of this, how do you see the global market situation playing out right now? And what's India's benefit here? We have been underperforming for a while.
A:

We are seeing a lot of uncertainties in the world right now, and for that reason, we do expect that equity markets broadly in the region, and that will include India, will be going through a bit of a period of volatility and may perform a little bit weakly over the next four to six weeks. That's including the move that we are seeing in rates, the uncertainty around oil, and also going into the midterm elections in the US. Typically, the seasonality around this period in September and October is very weak for equity markets, so we do think that will weigh on markets.

But if you step back a little bit and you look at the broader picture, you still have earnings in Asia going up very strongly, you've got valuations in Asia, which are pretty modest, you have a macro setup in a global context, which is still doing extremely well despite the rising rates, and you have investor positioning, which is relatively light at this point. So, all in all, the equity setup both in Asia and in regional markets is pretty positive.

Q: Most of the commentary this morning was all about what's happening with the US, Iran, and Russia-Ukraine, etc., all of that stuff, right? But the big one which has been powering markets and which has helped paper over the bulk of all of this, especially in the US, is the AI capex theme, which then trickles down to everything else, everywhere else. And Asia's been a huge beneficiary, not us, but countries north of us. What's the status check, or health check, in that sense, of that rally, if I can put it that way?
A:

We do look at the overall global equities as being somewhat AI versus non-AI because, at a global level, at an Asia level, and at the US level, pretty much half or more than half of the market is AI or AI-exposed stocks, and you are seeing a very separate performance across AI and non-AI stocks.

Now, for the AI stocks, at this point, it's become a question of how long this capex can be sustained, and for that to happen, we need to see better monetisation data, better business models from model companies, application companies, and software companies. These guys need to show that they are able to generate revenues from AI, and that will then trickle down into the hyperscalers, who will get the money from these model companies, and then they will pay the hardware companies who are producing all of this stuff.

So, the longer this AI boost can continue, the longer these AI stocks will continue to perform. At this point, with the data that we have today and with our expectations for the next few years, we are very comfortable that the AI stocks will probably continue to do well.

Q: Over the weekend, the other news point that came in was that Trump has signed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which allows 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian crude, which could probably mean that India as well as China could be in the dock. Do you think that the tariffs actually get activated, that is, higher tariffs, or is it just leverage that Trump can play with?
A:
We are not geopolitical analysts, so I wouldn't have a very strong view on this, but obviously, there's a lot of uncertainty around how the tariff situation as well as the oil situation is evolving.

The thing about oil prices right now is that there is a very strong chance that, at some point, the situation in Iran calms down, and oil prices suddenly gap lower. And a lot of investors are grappling with the risk that that might happen anytime soon, especially heading into the midterm elections.

But at the same time, the current supply-demand balance is extremely weak, and inventories are starting to run down across the world. So that is putting upward pressure on oil prices right now, but with the risk that they might come down anytime soon, investors are really very uncertain about what to do with oil prices here.

Q: US President Donald Trump's got big meetings this week, whether it's with regard to his Chinese counterpart, or he's probably meeting the Iranian president as well as various other Gulf leaders. Are you optimistic that things move in the right direction? There was a flash at the bottom of our screen that suggested that Trump's going to make a decision soon. With crude oil prices at these elevated levels, you have a Fed that's talking about another rate hike, and he's got the midterms due. Would you be more optimistic that decisions would be in favor of global equity markets?
A:

We analyse equities, so we are optimistic by nature. Yes, you are right that a lot of events are coming up, which involve Trump and various other world leaders, with the most important one perhaps being when President Xi visits him in Washington DC later this week. So, we'll see what comes out of that. From our conversations with investors, expectations about this meeting are not particularly high, so you could say that there is a higher chance that we could be surprised on the upside.

Q: Since we're speaking about the conference, and you said that there is some uncertainty that you're seeing, including the possibility of the Indian markets underperforming for the next four to six weeks as well. The one thing that can move our markets, apart from obviously our underlying fundamentals, which aren't particularly bad given the sort of uncertainty that we're seeing, is the return of FII flows. We've seen a lot of selling. Now that selling has reduced a little, but it's still selling. We haven't seen a lot of money flow into Indian markets. What is your case for FII money to come into the Indian markets, and what are you hearing from the sidelines of the conference there?
A:

We're here at the JP Morgan India Conference. We have over 1,200 delegates joining us, and more than 400 equity investors, many of whom are coming from foreign countries, including the US and Europe. And they are all here to try and figure out what's going on in the market and what they have been missing.

Because for the last 12 months, foreign investors haven't paid a lot of attention to India, and as you said, the growth numbers have started to pick up a little bit. This quarter's earnings reports were relatively strong, and investors are curious whether they are missing out on the building rally in the Indian equity market.
So, we'll see what comes out of the next two days of meetings, but investors are here with a cautious, optimistic stance, I would say.
Q: There is cautious optimism. What's your, you know, own feeling here, or the house view? Is there a rally that is building?
A:

We are neutral on India. As we discussed earlier, the AI stocks are still where we would prefer to be, where we still see the highest upside. If you look from an earnings perspective, you are getting 50% to 100% earnings growth even next year in various subsegments of the AI cohort. So, it's hard to kind of beat that.

So, we still think, from an allocation perspective, right now you're probably best allocated to: A, AI, and B, financials, as the rate move that we've been talking about happens, as many of these central banks globally start their hiking cycles or progress further through their hiking cycles, you would expect to see financials as a sector do well.
So that's kind of the barbell that we are recommending right now, and in that context, India somewhat falls into a neutral allocation for us.

title: JPMorgan sees 4-6 weeks of volatility in Asian markets, stays bullish on AI and financials
